title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF); Programming Languages (cs.PL)
abstract: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) decode is dominated by short, predominantly memory-bound kernels that make bursty use of on-chip execution resources and memory bandwidth. This paper introduces SubGPU Pipelining, a fine-grained, intra-GPU spatial execution model that cuts an operator graph into ordered contiguous segments, binds those segments to spatial stages backed by disjoint streaming-multiprocessor (SM) pools, and streams microbatches through the resulting schedule. Selecting the graph cuts, segment-to-stage binding, per-stage SM allocation, and microbatch size is a coupled optimization problem: each choice changes the overlap pattern, shared-resource contention, cache state, and execution times of the others.
We evaluate SubGPU Pipelining through both simulation and silicon experiment using the GPT-OSS 120B workload with 32-GPU B200 deployment settings. The analytical shared-resource simulator searches across SubGPU pipeline structures and batch sizes to map the per-user/per-GPU throughput Pareto frontier. At matched per-GPU throughput, the modeled SubGPU frontier provides up to 2.2x higher per-user throughput than temporal execution, and at matched per-user throughput it provides up to 1.9x higher per-GPU throughput. To test physical feasibility and further validate the simulation results, silicon experiments are performed, using one B200 GPU to emulate a 32-GPU B200 deployment. The experiment evaluates one selected two-stage pipeline configuration at global batch 2,048 using CUDA Green Contexts and TensorRT-LLM kernels. Results show that SubGPU Pipelining improves mean DRAM read-plus-write throughput from 71.8% to 83.6% of peak, and reduces the 36-layer decoder iteration time by 10.33%.

title: CuEVM: Scaling Smart Contract Execution on GPUs
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Databases (cs.DB)
abstract: Smart contracts on Ethereum blockchain process transactions worth billions of US dollars daily. They run on top of Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) which executes transactions sequentially. This execution model creates a performance bottleneck, especially for new blockchain workloads with large numbers of transactions, such as security testing. We present CuEVM, a GPU-native and semantically complete EVM execution engine that treats transaction execution as a massively parallel data processing problem. It employs novel data structures and GPU-aware scheduling to accelerate execution. Unlike prior works that transpile the contract and rely on a host CPU for many operations, CuEVM supports complete EVM semantics natively on the GPU. It passes 100% of the Ethereum VMTests and 96.2% of the full execution-test suite. On a single commodity GPU, CuEVM executes over 8 million ERC-20 transfers per second, outperforming existing baselines by up to two orders of magnitude. We build a smart contract fuzzer, called CuEVM-fuzz, on top of CuEVM. The fuzzer achieves over a million end-to-end executions per second, up to 23x and 4.8x higher than the state-of-the-art CPU-based and GPU-based baselines, respectively.

title: Recompute or Restore? Host-Tier KV for Multi-Model Agent Workflows on a Static-Graph NPU Serving Stack
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: Agent workflows issue dependent model calls that share long context prefixes, so serving them efficiently depends on reusing the key-value (KV) cache of those prefixes. On accelerators that compile model graphs ahead of time, however, the device KV budget is fixed, and prefixes evicted under load must be recomputed. Restoring them from host memory avoids this recomputation, but the transfer occupies the same engine thread as prefill and decode, so its benefit is not guaranteed. In this paper, we study when restoring beats recomputing on a commercial static-graph neural processing unit (NPU) stack (Rebellions ATOM+, vllm-rbln 0.10.2) that serves a Qwen3-8B planner on two cards and a Qwen3-0.6B executor on one. We first show that repeated prefill dominates planner work when default serving collapses: 89.5% of the executed planner prompt tokens had been materialized before. We then build a synchronous host-DRAM tier on the runtime's public KV copy calls, together with a scheduler-aware event model whose predictions are frozen before each test cohort. Experimental results show that the host tier raises workflow service-level objective (SLO) attainment from 22.8% to 100% and from 9.4% to 99.8% in the two tested overload conditions, and endpoint confirmation on two new seeds supports conservative load gains of 11.8% (chain) and 18.2% (fork), while mixed and bursty workloads remain seed-sensitive. The frozen model predicts median and 99th-percentile (P99) latency within its 15% tolerance in all 24 common-load conditions, including the 16-18% P99 increase that the tier causes for fork workflows, but it misorders three policy contrasts and overestimates the benefit of a cheaper store path (11% predicted against 3.1% measured). The trade-off therefore depends on runtime scheduling and transfer cost as well as cache capacity.

title: Sparse Matrix Multiplication Exponent 1.5 in the Low-bandwidth Model
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)
abstract:
We study sparse matrix multiplication in the low-bandwidth model: $n$ computers multiply two $n\times n$ matrices, and each computer can send and receive one $O(\log n)$-bit message per round. The input matrices are uniformly sparse, meaning that there are at most $d$ nonzero entries in each row and column, and the task is to compute a uniformly sparse part of their product.
In prior work, Gupta et al.~(SPAA 2022) presented an $O(d^{1.907})$-round algorithm over fields for this problem when the sparsity structure is globally known in advance (this is referred to as the supported setting). The upper bound was later improved to $O(d^{1.832})$ rounds.
In this work, we give a deterministic algorithm that solves this problem in $O(d^{3/2})$ rounds in the supported setting, improving the previous bounds over fields and semirings.

title: MoE Pretraining:Parallelism Layout Changes the Model, Not Quality
abstract: Large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are trained across many machines, and the way the work is split, the parallelism layout, often changes between runs: a job resumes on a different GPU count, a cluster is resized, or an ablation runs on a new setup. In exact arithmetic the layout should not matter, but in real arithmetic it changes the order in which numbers are added, and some MoE rules such as load balancing and expert capacity are often computed per machine. We ask whether the layout changes the trained MoE model. We pretrain the same small MoE language models (25M to 117M parameters, 20M FineWeb-Edu tokens) with the same seed, data and hyperparameters under 9 data-parallel and expert-parallel layouts, in fp32 on CPUs and fp16 on a GPU, and compare each run with the effect of a new random seed. Across 80 runs we find: (1) The layout does not change model quality, but it does change the model: final predictions differ about 80% as much as with a new seed, and over 90% of routing decisions differ. Any layout, a one-bit change to one weight, or a different CPU thread count has the same effect. (2) The cause is the router: decisions that flip are almost exactly those where two experts were nearly tied (AUC 0.97 to 1.00 in the first 16 steps). (3) More, smaller experts create more near-ties (2.7% with 8 experts, 23% with 64) and less reproducible routing (68% vs. 100% of decisions differ), but outputs do not drift further. (4) A dense model of the same active size is far more stable (0.12x the seed level in fp32, 0.58x in fp16), while the MoE reaches about 0.8x at both precisions and twice as fast. (5) When pretraining resumes on a new layout, timing matters: switching at 84% of pretraining barely changes the final model, while switching at 10%, just after warm-up, changes it substantially. We release code, run logs and data.

title: SoK: Design Choices in Tendermint BFT Consensus
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)
abstract: Tendermint is a consensus protocol that tolerates Byzantine faults, implemented first by the Tendermint Core engine and now by CometBFT. Realizing the protocol's separation of agreement from execution, the Application Blockchain Interface (ABCI) of these engines keeps consensus apart from the replicated application, so one engine can serve many independent proof-of-stake chains. A sustained body of research proposes changes that span the protocol's mechanisms, from vote dissemination to block proposal and reward distribution, yet to our knowledge no survey studies the protocol and these works as one family, and broader surveys do not take Tendermint as their subject. We describe the baseline, the protocol as consolidated from its original descriptions, by its design choices. Each is a decision, such as how votes spread or how proposers rotate, through which the baseline provides safety and liveness or another property under its fault and timing model. We classify each work by the design choice it renegotiates, that is, modifies or replaces, by the properties it strengthens or weakens, and by whether its result needs a stronger model. Taking a broader perspective on that classification, we group the surveyed works' solutions into a few threads of concern in the baseline, namely its performance, the accountability of its validators, and the protection of exploitable information. For each thread, we identify the recurring strategies that their approaches follow. Together, these threads and strategies describe the current state of research on the Tendermint family. Where the strategies leave gaps, we pose future directions, each as an open question under an explicit fault and timing model.

title: Smart Model Routing for Order-of-Magnitude LLM Cost Reduction
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) deliver the strongest response quality but carry per-token prices often more than an order of magnitude above those of smaller, task-adequate models. Smart model routing addresses this mismatch by assigning each query to the cheapest model expected to answer it adequately, rather than sending every request to the most capable, most expensive endpoint. This paper develops a formal cost-quality optimization framework for routing -- including a derived optimal threshold-policy structure, a calibration-versus-discrimination distinction, a cascade breakeven condition, and a sensitivity analysis over price ratio and traffic skew -- situates that framework against the principal routing architectures and the signals used to estimate query difficulty, and works through a numerical example showing how a calibrated router can reduce blended inference cost by roughly an order of magnitude relative to an always-frontier deployment under specific, stated pricing and traffic assumptions, reporting both the gross reduction from routing policy alone and the net figure with the router's own overhead priced in. We situate this figure against the range reported by published routing systems (roughly 2x to frontier-level accuracy at one-fifth the cost), and close with the practical risks -- under- and over-routing, aggregate quality constraints masking segment-level harm, calibration without discrimination, calibration drift, prompt injection into routing signals, and operational failures such as tier outages and multi-provider price variation -- that determine whether the savings materialize in production. The analysis is primarily analytical, complemented by a GSM8K evaluation of the cascade framework (Section 5), validated (Section 5.2); extending the evaluation across tasks and model families is future work.

title: NVIDIA Vera: A Microarchitecture-Level Comparison with Grace, Turin, and Granite Rapids
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract:
The majority of new HPC systems are centered around NVIDIA, AMD, or Intel CPUs. Vera is NVIDIA's latest data-center CPU, including its first custom data-center core design, Olympus. This paper investigates Vera in comparison to AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids, using NVIDIA Grace as a baseline. We navigate up the performance ladder, from microbenchmarks that isolate performance metrics, through NAS kernels and miniapps, to single-socket performance of a range of scientific codes.
We find that Vera achieves the best performance of the architectures evaluated in most codes tested, and that this gain is primarily attributed to its high memory bandwidth, effective Spatial Multithreading implementation, and low-latency memory subsystem aided by the architecture's predictive structures. While Vera represents a major leap over its predecessor, we show that its comparatively modest floating-point performance trails Intel and AMD in a small number of compute-bound workloads reflecting NVIDIA's GPU focus for such workloads.

title: Starscream: Reimagining LLM Sharding on AMD Instinct GPUs with GPU Partitioning
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: As GPU accelerators grow larger to meet rising compute demands, they exhibit increasingly pronounced non-uniform memory access (NUMA) characteristics that challenge existing LLM frameworks. Chiplet-based architectures provide a practical path to larger GPUs while mitigating manufacturing yield constraints. Modern GPUs such as AMD Instinct MI300X employs such a multi-die design, and further offer GPU partitioning capabilities, partitioning a single physical GPU into multiple logical devices with NUMA-aware memory domains, promising faster kernel launches, and reduced memory access latencies with improved locality. However, current parallelization strategies, designed for homogeneous GPU topologies, when applied under partitioning, extend its unidimensional sharding causing significant performance degradation. Three bottlenecks emerge: (1) memory redundancy; (2) arithmetic intensity collapse; (3) communication overhead from flat collectives. We present Starscream, a rethinking of LLM sharding for the chiplet era. Rather than stretching inter-GPU sharding thinner, Starscream adds intra-GPU sharding along an orthogonal dimension, grounded in three foundational principles: kernel shape preservation, memory redundancy elimination, and communication overhead minimization. These principles form the basis for extending any sharding strategy into the partitioning regime. We demonstrate their effectiveness using tensor parallelism as a case study. On AMD MI300X and MI355X, exploiting partitioning capabilities yields up to 4x speedup for attention and 1.43x for fused GEMMs compared to chiplet-oblivious baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of chiplet-aware designs. Starscream's principles generalize across sharding strategies and future architectures.

title: Plurality Consensus for $h$-Majority via First-Repetition Rules
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)
abstract: In the h-Majority dynamics, each of n agents holds one of k opinions and, in every synchronous round, observes the opinions of h agents chosen independently and uniformly at random and adopts a most frequent one among them, breaking ties uniformly at random. Let M_0 be the initial number of agents holding the most frequent opinion, and Delta_0 its bias, its lead over the second most frequent opinion. We show that, for every sample size h >= 3, if Delta_0 >= L sqrt(M_0 log n) max{1, n/(h^2 M_0)} for a sufficiently large constant L, then h-Majority reaches consensus on the initially most frequent opinion within O((1 + n/(h^2 M_0)) log n) rounds with high probability. This is the time bound proved for the DejaVu dynamics with h samples (arXiv:2604.03648); our bias condition is that of DejaVu when h >= sqrt(n/M_0), and larger by a factor sqrt(n/(h^2 M_0)) otherwise. Our main contribution, the analysis of one round, rests on a comparison principle: among all rules that read the same observations and treat opinions symmetrically, plurality maximizes the difference between the probability of outputting the most frequent opinion and that of outputting any fixed competitor. We apply it to the rule that adopts the first opinion repeated among h-1 observations, and otherwise the h-th observation: its output law is the law of the new opinion of a random agent after one round of DejaVu with h-1 samples. Hence, in expectation, one round of h-Majority widens the gap between the most frequent opinion and each competitor at least as much as that round of DejaVu, whose analysis we use as a black box. Independently and concurrently, d'Amore, Rybicki, Shimizu, Shiraga and Vacus (arXiv:2610.40562) obtained, among other results, the same time bound under the weaker bias condition of DejaVu, with a different analysis of one round and a martingale analysis over many rounds.

title: Accelerating Distributed Variational Quantum Computing over Wireless Networks with Incentive Mechanism Design
abstract: Distributed variational quantum computing (DVQC) appears as the emerging paradigm to address the limitations of near-term quantum devices by decomposing large parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) into smaller subcircuits executed across multiple quantum processors. In this context, how to incentivize quantum processors to participate actively is crucial for accelerating DVQC, yet remains largely unexplored in the literature. To address this significant gap, we propose a novel two-stage incentive framework for wireless DVQC. In the first stage, we minimize processor-side energy cost via a joint optimization of subcircuit parameters, number of noise measurements, and transmit power, efficiently solved using block coordinate descent (BCD) and successive convex approximation (SCA). In the second stage, we maximize aggregator-side system utility by selecting an optimal subset of processors based on their optimized energy costs derived from the first stage, formulating a non-convex combinatorial selection problem addressed using the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). Extensive numerical experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our DVQC framework achieves training and testing performance comparable to centralized quantum computing in terms of accuracy and loss, with similar convergence behavior on MNIST and slightly slower initial convergence on CIFAR-10. Moreover, our optimization approach consistently outperforms baseline schemes in energy efficiency and system utility, revealing a strong synergy between processor-level energy minimization and incentive-driven processor selection, where reduced energy costs directly enhances a processor's likelihood of selection and contributes to higher overall system utility.

title: Fast Serverless LLM Cold Starts by Sharing and Prewarming Startup Work
abstract: When a serverless LLM platform launches a model worker on demand, the cold start lasts roughly a minute, yet only 5-11% of it is spent loading weights. Most of the remainder goes to compilation, memory profiling and runtime setup, which each server performs again even though the outcome is identical across servers or independent of the model. We present Cairn. The server that is first to start a model publishes the weights and engine artifacts to a CXL memory pool shared across the cluster, and the remaining servers read them in place. Model-independent setup is completed ahead of time inside warm containers, and a template process replaces each container as soon as it is used. With ServerlessLLM on vLLM v0.20, six models from 1B to 14B, and two servers that share an emulated CXL pool, Cairn speeds up cold starts by 4.1-5.2x on servers without a checkpoint of their own and reduces median TTFT on a request stream by 64%.

title: GC-MoE on SM120: Overlapping Expert-Parallel Token Dispatch with Warp-Level FP8xFP4 Block-Scaled MMA on Consumer Blackwell
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level this http URL::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.

title: MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance
abstract: Modern ML frameworks execute models using the kernel-per-operator paradigm, which runs each operator as a separate GPU kernel. This paradigm is modular, since developers can compose various kernel implementations and profile each kernel in isolation. However, this paradigm enforces dependencies at the granularity of entire kernels, which places a barrier between dependent kernels. These barriers cause streaming multiprocessors to idle, serialize computation and communication, and prevent a kernel from prefetching its weights while the preceding kernel runs. Megakernels remove kernel barriers by fusing the operators of an entire layer or model into a single kernel, but they give up the modularity of the kernel-per-operator paradigm. In this work, we ask whether a kernel-per-operator ML framework can perform on par with megakernels. Our key insight is that removing kernel barriers does not require fusing kernels. We develop MegaOps, a framework that launches dependent kernels on separate CUDA streams and enforces each dependency on individual tiles of the intermediate tensor that the producer kernel writes and the consumer kernel reads. Since kernels synchronize on data tiles instead of on each other's thread blocks, any two kernels that adopt the same data tiling can be composed without modifying either kernel. We evaluate MegaOps on dense Llama3 and Qwen3 models on single H100, A100, and L40 GPUs and on multi-GPU servers with 4$\times$A100 and 8$\times$H100. Our MegaOps framework matches the throughput of hand-tuned ThunderKittens megakernels, and achieves 1.09$\times$-1.10$\times$ the decode throughput and 0.98$\times$-1.10$\times$ the prefill throughput of the best-performing baseline, while reusing existing Triton, cuBLAS, and cuDNN kernels.

title: Parallel Computing Systems for the Optimal Selection of Process Equipment
abstract: This monograph addresses the optimal selection of equipment for chemical-engineering systems of multiproduct batch plants, a large-scale NP-hard discrete optimization problem in which, for each processing stage, a unit of standard size must be chosen so that the total capital cost of the equipment is minimized while the system remains operable and produces the required products within a given time horizon. We present the mathematical model of system operation and analyze its computational properties. We then develop a sequential branch-and-bound algorithm and its parallel versions for shared-memory systems (OpenMP), distributed-memory clusters (MPI, master-worker), and graphics processing units (CUDA), including recursive and iterative tree traversal, shared-memory optimization, and branch-divergence reduction. To overcome the exponential growth of the run time, we propose a hybrid metaheuristic in which Ant Colony Optimization finds a feasible initial solution and Simulated Annealing improves it, and we implement it on GPUs with thousands of independent threads. Finally, we propose random, constant, and multi-constant approaches to tuning the parameters of the ant colony algorithm based on statistical analysis of many parallel runs, and we study the program on GPUs of three generations and on nodes with several GPUs. Computational experiments on multi-core processors, clusters, and GPUs show that the parallel hybrid algorithm finds solutions within 0.01% of the branch-and-bound optimum in tens of seconds instead of tens of hours.

title: Smoothed Analysis for Distributed MIS
abstract:
We study smoothed analysis of the distributed Maximal Independent Set (MIS) problem. Luby's algorithm computes an MIS in $O(\log n)$ rounds, while the recent $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ lower bound of Khoury and Schild (2026) shows that it is nearly optimal even in the LOCAL model. We ask whether small random perturbations can overcome this worst-case barrier.
Given an arbitrary base graph $G$ on $n$ nodes, we consider the smoothed graph $\mathcal{G}_s=G\triangle G(n,p)$, where $G(n,p)$ is an independent random graph and $\triangle$ denotes symmetric difference. Thus, each possible edge is independently toggled with probability $p$.
We establish nearly tight bounds on the smoothing needed for faster distributed MIS. For every base graph $G$, when $p=\beta\ln n/n$ for a sufficiently large constant $\beta$, a randomized LOCAL algorithm, given only $\mathcal{G}_s$, computes an MIS of $\mathcal{G}_s$ in $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ rounds with high probability. This is almost quadratically faster than the worst-case lower bound. Conversely, if $p\le(1/2-\delta)\ln n/n$ for a fixed constant $\delta>0$, there exists a base graph on which every randomized LOCAL MIS algorithm requires $\Omega(\log n/\log\log n)$ rounds on the smoothed graph. Hence, the smoothing parameter required for this speedup is optimal up to a constant factor.
These results show that smoothed analysis can overcome worst-case lower-bound barriers for distributed local graph problems.

title: Snoopie: A Multi-GPU Communication Profiler and Visualizer
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: With data movement becoming one of the most expensive bottlenecks in computing, the need for profiling tools to analyze communication becomes crucial for effectively scaling multi-GPU applications. While existing profiling tools including first-party software by GPU vendors are robust and excel at capturing compute operations within a single GPU, support for monitoring GPU-GPU data transfers and calls issued by communication libraries is currently inadequate. To fill these gaps, we introduce Snoopie, an instrumentation-based multi-GPU communication profiling tool built on NVBit, capable of tracking peer-to-peer transfers and GPU-centric communication library calls. To increase programmer productivity, Snoopie can attribute data movement to the source code line and the data objects involved. It comes with multiple visualization modes at varying granularities, from a coarse view of the data movement in the system as a whole to specific instructions and addresses. Our case studies demonstrate Snoopie's effectiveness in monitoring data movement, locating performance bugs in applications, and understanding concrete data transfers abstracted beneath communication libraries. The tool is publicly available at this https URL.

title: SS-HSDP: Efficient and Flexible Sharded Data Parallelism via Runtime-Update Decoupling
abstract: Sharded data parallelism enables memory-efficient training of large models. While efficient training kernels favor packed, kernel-specific data layouts, optimizers may require variant data structures as optimization units. Existing sharded data-parallel frameworks couple these two choices, limiting runtime efficiency and optimization flexibility. To address this, we present \textbf{\our}, a training framework that separates runtime parameters from update parameters, allowing computation layouts and optimization units to be organized independently. Through shared data views and hierarchical sharding, \our supports this separation while avoiding redundant data movement. This design supports a broad range of optimizers, including matrix-based methods such as Muon, and performance optimizations such as fully zero-copy execution. Experiments on video and language model workloads with MXFP8 training show that \our achieves higher Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) than FSDP2, veScale-FSDP, and Megatron-FSDP. At 128 GPUs, MFU improves by up to 21.7\% over the fastest evaluated baseline, with comparable or lower peak memory usage.

title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: We introduce CABOT, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an active computing medium. In the classical Look-Compute-Move (LCM) model every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid once per robot. CABOT strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the grid holds a state from a finite set Q, the states evolve synchronously under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the Look operation returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 1, without multiplicity detection and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |Q|, rather than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required. On an inert floor (|Q| = 1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected, configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row, fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and indicate the range of the model.

title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
abstract: Efficient batch execution of agent tasks is critical to LLM training and development workflows, including benchmark evaluation, synthetic-data generation, and RL rollouts. Since these tasks alternate between LLM inference and environment interaction, we present coordinated optimizations to reduce batch makespan, the time required to complete all tasks in a batch. For hybrid LLMs, a workload-based resource model guides GPU-memory allocation between key-value (KV) cache and recurrent state and provides a reference sample concurrency to exploit parallelism while limiting recomputation. Trajectory-aware routing and scheduling promote cache reuse while balancing worker load. Under constrained environment capacity, we decouple sample admission from environment execution and introduce Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling (CAAS), which prioritizes long chains using observed progress to shorten the batch tail. Controlled replay combines actual inference with recorded environment responses and durations for ablations of individual optimizations. Live evaluations with Ling-3.0-Flash and Ling-3.1-Flash on the BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas benchmarks demonstrate makespan reductions of 10.4% to 65.0%, while evaluation scores remain aligned. Furthermore, these methods have been successfully applied to training and evaluation workflows for the Ling-3.x model series, accelerating the model-development cycle.

title: Locality Meets Interference: Structure and Scheduling in Radio Multicasting
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)
abstract: We study multipoint-to-multipoint multicasting in synchronous radio networks with unknown participant locations and unrestricted message aggregation. Let $n$ be the network size, $k$ the number of participants, and $d$ their hop diameter. A supplied distance-two coloring with $C$ colors yields completion within $(C-1)d+1$ slots and at most $nk$ transmissions. In unit disk graphs, coordinates, one-hop neighbor data, and a common degree bound $\Delta_0$ suffice for a $15(\Delta_0+1)$-color schedule. A known fixed separation bound permits optimal deterministic $\Theta(d)$ completion from coordinates alone. Without geometric data, strong selectivity gives $O(d\min\{n,(\Delta_0+1)^2\log n\})$ slots when $n$ is known. Independent random transmission gives $O((\Delta_0+1)(d+\log(k/\eta)))$ slots with failure probability at most $\eta$; for fixed $\Delta_0$, this simplifies to $O(d+\log(1/\eta))$. A star construction shows that the logarithmic term is necessary for this random rule when the degree grows. We extend color schedules to fixed deletions and subgraphs connected over bounded windows of cycles. Separate conditional reductions preserve additive costs under diameter guessing and control parameter-table and cluster preprocessing. Finally, a counterexample shows that pruning and reranking a breadth-first tree can destroy interference-free delivery. For one-hop designated delivery with receiver degree at most $b$, we prove that the optimal schedule length equals the chromatic number of an associated conflict graph and is at most $2b-1$, with matching examples.

title: PACER: GPU Excursion Management for ML Workloads
abstract:
Variability is an inherent characteristic of modern GPU systems, arising from a combination of process variation, dynamic environmental conditions, and power management decisions. Prior work has characterized inter-GPU variability and found consistent performance differences across GPUs. However, we observe that modern workloads, particularly large language models (LLMs), exhibit significant intra-GPU variability. Their short-running kernels interact poorly with the coarse granularity of dynamic power management mechanisms, leading to unpredictable performance.
A key source of this intra-GPU transient variability is power excursions, also referred to as electrical design power peaks (EDP$_{p}$), where power temporarily exceeds the GPU's rated power limits. While power management mechanisms are designed to ensure reliable operation despite the presence of EDP$_{p}$ sustained power peaks cause throttling that detrimentally impacts overall application performance. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to characterize the magnitude and frequency of EDP$_{p}$, showing that frequent, significant power overshoots are especially common in ML workloads, which combine high power draw, short kernels, and rapidly changing compute demands. To address this, we design and leverage hardware and firmware mechanisms to provide consistent power management behavior that reduces intra-GPU variability due to EDP$_{p}$ and improves overall performance. We evaluate our techniques across a range of popular workloads. Our approach improves performance by 3-12% over state-of-the-art GPU power management and comes within 3% of an oracular solution.

title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$\mu$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering.
We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).

title: FIRE: Failure Isolation and Reliability for Production-Connected Experiments at Scale
subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Pre-production changes are usually tested in isolated environments to prevent their side effects from reaching production. Some record-and-replay platforms allow a production-connected mode: candidate changes receive recorded production requests while selected downstream calls reach production dependencies. This improves fidelity before deployment, but it also introduces reliability risks. At hyperscale, experimental traffic can fan out across shared services, trigger latent defects, or send malformed input to systems serving user requests. In this paper, we show how production-connected experimentation can operate reliably in a large-scale recommendation serving system. To contain downstream effects without sacrificing realistic dependency behavior, the platform uses three complementary guardrails. Isolated tiers redirect replay traffic away from shared dependencies where replication is practical. Dependency monitors observe downstream health and experiment-attributed errors and terminate experiments after sustained violations. Traffic pinning limits experimental calls to a designated subset of downstream workers when full replication would require scarce capacity. Isolated ranking tiers process billions of replayed requests per day using under 1% of the corresponding serving capacity. Over 90 days, these tiers experienced more than 200,000 abnormal worker exits without directly affecting production-serving workers. During a separate three-month window, dependency monitors cancelled approximately 5% of experiments for the measured ranking service and accounted for 87% of its cancellations. Dependency-aware triggering also reduced code-review experiment executions by 25%. These results show that high-fidelity, production-connected experimentation can operate at scale when downstream effects are isolated where possible, bounded where necessary, and continuously monitored and attributed.

title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments. XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback. We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26-3.75 times the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at this https URL.

title: Instruction-Aware Transfer of GPU Implementation Crossovers: a Tensor-Product Discontinuous Galerkin Operator on GB200, H100, and A100
subjects: Performance (cs.PF); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: We compare up to six implementations of an FP64 tensor-product discontinuous Galerkin operator at p = 7-1023 on GB200, H100, and A100 with fixed numerics, input, and code. The fastest path is machine dependent: at p = 511, a fused-epilogue GEMM path is 5.0% faster than a fused Tensor Core kernel on GB200 and 6.9% slower on A100. Nominal-peak scaling reproduces the A100 ranking but fails on H100, where the cost of FP64 arithmetic in the profiler-defined FP64 budget depends on the instruction. We therefore price each issued instruction at its architecture-dependent cost in that budget, using a calibration-side counter profile and one derived calibration factor per kernel, with no fit to the target. A retrospective leave-one-GPU-out evaluation, holding out target timings and counters but not the model form, transfers the p >= 511 path times with 1.9% median error at the common MMA shape, and the direction of the crossover at the H100 shape. Restricting the streaming multiprocessors of one A100, with nothing fitted, reproduces the A100-to-GB200 reversal. At roduction-relevant orders the model does not resolve the fastest fused path; the result identifies the crossover mechanism.

title: Read Once, Answer Many: Parallel Prompting for Shared-Context LLM Inference
subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: LLM workloads sometimes ask many independent questions about the same long document, as in document QA, data labeling and LLM-based evaluation. Prefix caching removes the redundant prefill shared by these queries, but each decode step still reads the document's key-value (KV) cache once per question, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and scales with the number of questions. We present Parallel Prompting, which decodes P questions as P independent streams of a single request all at once, fixing this issue. In our method, every step reads the shared document once for all P streams, and a stream-id attention mask, evaluated inside the attention kernel, keeps each answer conditioned only on the document and its own question. We implement Parallel Prompting in SGLang by adding about 80 lines to three existing files and a small engine package; the mask needs no dense tensor, and every decode step has a fixed shape that is captured as a CUDA graph. With CodeLlama-7B, 8k-16k-token documents and 64-256 questions per document, Parallel Prompting is 3.7x faster than stock SGLang with its FlashInfer backend on an A100 and 5.9-6.0x faster on an RTX A6000, on two SGLang releases, including the most recent release. Timed on identical inputs, it is faster than stock SGLang in all 144 runs (2 GPUs x 2 releases x 6 workloads x 6 input sets). Code: this https URL

title: A Parallel Greedy Algorithm for Maximal b-Matching in Hypergraphs
subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: We present \parallelBatchBMatch, a parallel batch-vote algorithm for maximal $b$-matching in hypergraphs. The algorithm is deterministic for a given ordering of edges and produces the same output as the sequential greedy algorithm, i.e., the lexicographically first maximal $b$-matching. Under a uniformly random priority order it performs $O(m')$ expected work in the binary fork--join model, where $m'$ is the number of pins, the total number of vertex--edge incidences. The algorithm performs at most $m$ rounds for every priority order, where $m$ is the number of edges. Every round of the algorithm has $O(\log^2 m')$ depth with high probability, and thus the total depth of the algorithm is $O(m \log^2 m')$ with high probability. We implement the parallel algorithm in CUDA and evaluate it on real-world hypergraphs with capacities $b \in \{1, 3, 5\}$. The parallel algorithm computes the same matchings as the greedy algorithms and for the case of $b = 5$ it is up to $19.07$ times faster than the existing state-of-the art greedy algorithm.

title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.

title: LoCoJAX: Host-Local Coordination for Small-Model RL on TPUs
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) increasingly targets small language models, and executing these workloads efficiently across multiple accelerators requires effective coordination. On TPUs, Pathways-based RL uses a single controller to coordinate computation across hosts. This execution model is effective for large models, but its coordination computational costs are harder to amortize when small models repeatedly invoke short computations. To characterize these computational costs, we sweep dense models from 0.6B to 405B parameters on TPU v7x under a decode-heavy workload and measure how host and network computational overhead vary with model size. At 0.6B, host orchestration occupies 36% of step time and network communication 2%, whereas for large models, estimated network computational costs dominate the non-compute time. Motivated by these findings, we present Local Coordination JAX (LoCoJAX), which implements local rollout and reward processing on each TPU host with synchronous global training. In controlled comparisons against a tuned and optimized Pathways baseline on Qwen3-0.6B across three workloads and 8-64 TPU v7x chips, its colocated mode (LoCoJAX-CO) is 1.3-3.6x faster per step; on GSM8K, it completes a step faster on 8 chips than Pathways does on 64. Finally, a Ray-managed disaggregated mode (LoCoJAX-DA) overlaps rollout and training on separate hosts, and placement experiments establish when this overlap compensates for dividing devices and transferring weights: only when rollout dominates the step and receives most of the hosts. On NuminaMath-CoT at 256 chips, giving rollout 75% of hosts cuts step time by about 15% compared with LoCoJAX-CO.

title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it.
We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
subjects: Databases (cs.DB); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract:
As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle.
We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not.
On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.

title: Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of Sparse Convolution
subjects: Performance (cs.PF); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Deep neural networks for image processing are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge devices such as drones, medical systems, and smartphones, where limited computational resources and memory bandwidth pose significant challenges for efficient inference. Pruning during training often produces highly sparse convolutional kernels, offering the potential to significantly reduce computation and memory requirements. However, exploiting this sparsity efficiently at runtime remains challenging due to irregular memory access patterns and workload imbalance across processing elements. In this work, we investigate the standard convolution with sparse weights and analyze its performance characteristics through roofline analysis, showing that a 3 x 3 sparse convolution achieves an arithmetic intensity of approximately 10 FLOP/byte compared to roughly 96 FLOP/byte for its dense counterpart. We propose techniques for an efficient sparse convolution at high sparsities. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach achieves upto 1.65x speedup as compared to dense convolution on NVIDIA A100 and upto 1.52x on NVIDIA Jetson Nano (Tegra X1) , motivating further exploration of direct convolution as a practical path to efficient sparse inference on modern accelerators/edge devices.

title: Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: On-device inference requires kernels that make effective use of local accelerators. Efficient training and evaluation of models that generate Apple Metal kernels benefit from native macOS tools and concurrent agent sessions. These sessions alternate between model requests, development commands, and GPU execution, leaving GPU capacity idle for much of a rollout. We present Metal Sandbox, infrastructure that combines restricted per-instance file access, native command execution, and command-level scheduling across interconnected Macs. Each agent retains its workspace and private development environment. Parallel commands can run concurrently, while serial commands share one execution slot per node; eligible waiting commands can migrate to available Macs and return results to the original agent. Integration with Harbor supports task execution, automatic verification, and rollout collection through a common workflow. Controlled experiments on four Mac mini M4 nodes achieve $1.68\times$--$2.05\times$ gains in command throughput under concentrated demand. Sixteen static agent traces give an estimated $2.14\times$ sustained-throughput gain for four sessions per node versus one, assuming continuously replenished sessions and unchanged mean durations. Replaying these measured traces under dynamic scheduling reduces mean tool waiting by 18.8% and batch elapsed time by 22.3%, assuming unchanged phase durations. Metal Sandbox and its Harbor integration are open-source on GitHub.

title: Tideway: Phase-Aware Tiered Memory Management for MoE Inference on Consumer Devices
abstract:
Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly becoming a dominant paradigm for AI applications. Recently, there is a growing demand to deploy large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models locally on consumer PCs to balance data privacy, API costs, and inference efficiency. However, unlike datacenter servers with abundant DRAM, consumer devices are tightly constrained in both GPU VRAM and host RAM, forcing massive MoE weights to spill across VRAM, host RAM, and SSD. Under such spilling, we observe that existing systems fail to fully utilize this memory hierarchy, treating the tiers as independent caches and thrashing in inference.
We present TIDEWAY, a system for efficient inference of large MoE models on memory-constrained consumer devices. Our core insight is to manage host RAM and GPU VRAM as a unified memory pool. Within this pool, TIDEWAY couples phase-aware memory layouts, which adapt to the distinct access patterns of prefill and decode, with an execution engine that optimizes CUDA Graph execution under expert paging. Our evaluations on representative consumer hardware with frontier MoE models demonstrate that TIDEWAY significantly outperforms state-of-the-art systems. On average, TIDEWAY achieves speedups of 1.97x in end-to-end latency and 2.40x in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), along with 1.61x higher decode throughput against the fastest baseline.
Our source code is publicly available at this https URL .

title: Towards Runtime-Aware Observability for Java Virtual Threads
abstract: OS-level observability tools join application requests to kernel events through the OS thread ID, assuming that a unit of work occupies one OS thread until it completes. Java virtual threads break this assumption: many virtual threads are multiplexed onto a few carrier threads, so a stable thread ID hides a changing unit of work, and the join fails silently. Existing virtual-thread-aware channels republish context or identity on every mount and unmount, and the JVMTI-based one pays this cost for the lifetime of the JVM, whether or not an observer is attached. We bind a 64-byte off-heap trace buffer to each virtual thread, at a fixed address for its lifetime, and publish the address to eBPF consumers through four USDT probes in a patched OpenJDK; a re-implemented JVMTI channel over the same buffer serves as a controlled comparison. The four-probe design attributed all 768 test markers correctly on both the content and the identity plane, while the naive two-probe design silently misattributes trace context. With no consumer attached, publication costs at most about 33 ns per transition; the remaining dormant cost is buffer allocation, about 0.37 microseconds per virtual thread, which is negligible on transition-heavy workloads but nearly doubles the cost of a creation-only microbenchmark. The JVMTI channel costs about 20% on transition-heavy workloads and about 1.8 microseconds per virtual thread on the creation-only one. We also show that, of the two update strategies OTEP 4947 permits, only in-place rewriting guarded by the record's valid flag is sound for readers that cache the record's address, as lifecycle-event readers do.

title: LLMRunner: Closed Workload Model Performance Testing Framework for LLM Servings
abstract:
Performance testing large language model (LLM) serving engines is a crucial requirement considering the criticality of the infrastructure for deploying conversational AI at scale. Most of the benchmarking tools used to carryout performance evaluation of LLM serving do not capture realistic workload orchestration unlike closed workload performance testing infrastructure used in other domains such as web and database engines. For example, state-of-the-art LLM benchmarks for performance testing model traffic as streams of independent single-turn and stand-alone requests omitting the end-user behavior such as think-time between conversational turns. We present LLMRunner, a performance tester for LLM serving that addresses this gap by providing a framework to generate realistic load consisting of multi-turn conversations with configurable end-user parameters such as number of users in the workload loop, think-time distributions etc. Moreover, LLMRunner provides declarative matrix-sweep experiment plans, integrated GPU and KV-cache monitoring, and an automated artifact collection and plotting subsystem.
We use LLMRunner to comparatively analyze the performance of LLM serving when NVIDIA CUDA Unified Virtual Memory (UVM) is used as a drop-in replacement memory allocator for the Key-Value cache (KV-Cache). Our test demonstrates that UVM incurs no measurable throughput or latency penalty compared to the baseline memory allocation technique for non-oversubscription scenarios.

title: Towards Automated Recommendation of Steady-State Detection Algorithms for Software Performance Benchmarks
abstract: Steady-state detection is a central step in software performance benchmarking, yet different detection methods rely on different assumptions and may perform best on different execution profiles. This paper formulates steady-state detection as an algorithm-recommendation problem: given a benchmark time series, predict which of two complementary detectors is more appropriate. The first, CP-SSD, identifies steady state through changepoint-based segmentation of the execution trace, whereas the second, KB-KSSD, uses a kernel-based approach to identify stable behaviour. We propose a data-driven recommender that characterises benchmark time series using automatically extracted features and combines supervised prediction with information derived from groups of time series exhibiting similar behaviour. The approach is evaluated on 407 labelled benchmark time series for which one of the two detectors can be identified as preferable with respect to a reference steady-state index. The proposed recommender selects the better detector correctly for 72.97% of the series, compared with 62.65% when always selecting the detector that performs best most often, corresponding to an absolute improvement of 10.32 percentage points. Paired statistical testing and bootstrap confidence intervals support this improvement. A comparison with a recommender using time-series features alone shows that the cluster-derived information mainly improves interpretability rather than predictive accuracy. Recommendations also remain highly stable when the unsupervised representation is learned from either the labelled subset or the full collection of 5,860 time series. These results demonstrate the feasibility of per-series steady-state detector recommendation while highlighting the need for broader labelled data, particularly for execution profiles favouring the changepoint-based detector.

title: Control-Flow Profiling for Workload Representativeness
abstract:
Workload characterization in performance engineering often replaces expensive target executions with lower-cost proxies, including reduced datasets, miniapps, and training inputs. Such substitutions require empirical verification that the proxy faithfully exercises the target's dynamic execution behavior. This paper presents an address-keyed control-flow profiling methodology and tool suite designed to evaluate workload representativeness directly from compiled, unmodified binaries. We pair time-ordered basic-block vector (BBV) recurrence analysis with exp-branchprof, an experimental Valgrind tool that captures five orthogonal structural profile families spanning branch direction bias, four-bit global history contexts, dynamic indirect targets, function call transitions, and intraprocedural CFG edges.
Our method compares weighted event distributions from two executions of the same binary. It reports support coverage, reference event-mass coverage, distribution distance, entropy-derived quantities, and phase structure, rather than claiming that a single similarity score certifies a proxy. We validate the tool with exact-oracle microbenchmarks across AArch64 and x86-64, covering conditional and inverted exits, calls, returns, direct and indirect jumps, and forked processes. We then apply the workflow to SPEC CPU2017 and CPU2026 train/reference pairs and seven refrate/refspeed pairs. The corpus contains both close matches and cases where a shorter execution reaches much of the same code but misses substantial target, callgraph, CFG, or BBV event mass. The accompanying artifact supports the same analysis for proprietary workload/proxy pairs without requiring raw PC-level profiles to leave the collection environment.

title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Performance (cs.PF); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

title: SPEC CPU2026 Under the Microscope: Programs, Phases, and Samples
abstract: SPEC CPU2026, the latest generation of the SPEC CPU benchmarks, is set to become the standard benchmark suite in computer architecture research, where new designs are often evaluated through sampled simulation with tools such as SimPoint. Existing characterizations of the suite focus on whole-run averages, which reveal neither how behavior changes within a run nor how well sampling captures it. We characterize CPU2026 on real hardware at three levels: programs, phases, and samples. At the program level, we report whole-run metrics and top-down bottleneck classes for all four suites and examine how they change with workload size, compiler version, and platform, across machines with three different instruction set architectures: x86, Arm, and RISC-V. Notably, changing only the compiler version can halve or nearly double the IPC of individual benchmarks. At the phase level, we track hardware counters every 10 ms over all 90 SPECrate inputs, identify recurring patterns of time-varying behavior, and divide the inputs into three groups: steady, multi-phase, and bursty. More than half of the inputs show time-varying behavior, and IPC within a single input can vary by more than an order of magnitude. At the sample level, we validate SimPoint against hardware measurements of every interval it can select. SimPoint is accurate on steady inputs, but its error reaches 43% on the others, and changing only the random seed spreads the error of one input over a range of 58 percentage points. Keeping SimPoint's clusters but choosing each representative by measured CPI brings every input within 2.6%, so the error comes from the choice of representatives, not from the clustering. We conclude with practical recommendations on sampling strategy for CPU2026, which give researchers a deeper understanding of the suite and show where additional simulation effort is needed to keep sampled results accurate.

title: To Race or Not to Race? Exploiting Performance Variability in Mixed-Integer Programming via Root-Gated Resource Allocation
abstract:
Mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver runtimes vary substantially across random seeds. Parallel replication exploits this variability but can waste computational resources when applied indiscriminately. We investigate whether information from an ordinary solve can guide this allocation decision.
We formulate replication under a finite deadline, establish an exact relationship between runtime dispersion and the value of independent searches, and analyze delayed replication and imperfect allocation decisions. Using 101,615 seeded SCIP runs, we examine the association between root-LP dual degeneracy and replication value. We then introduce a non-invasive root-gated policy that preserves the original solver trajectory and launches three additional seeded processes when a root dual-degeneracy indicator reaches a fixed threshold.
In a prospective two-hour experiment on 130 paired instances, root-gated racing proves optimality on 77 instances (59.23%), versus 73 (56.15%) for both Single and unconditional Race-4, while reducing active worker-process occupancy by 43.00% relative to unconditional racing. These findings demonstrate the promise of selective parallel resource allocation without solver-source modifications.

title: metalSPARSE: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for Apple Silicon GPUs
subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.

title: CAFIN: CUDA-accelerated Adaptive Fisher Information Matrix Network Optimization via GPU-Native Kernel Fusion
abstract: Second-order optimizers improve deep neural network training using curvature information, but their practical efficiency is limited by GPU execution overhead. AdaFisher reduces Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) approximation costs through diagonal Kronecker structures and exponential moving averages, yet its PyTorch implementation requires sequential CUDA kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. We introduce CAFIN, a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that improves AdaFisher execution efficiency without changing its optimization formulation. The proposed approach progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, exponential moving average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels. Shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations further reduce memory traffic and intermediate allocations. Experiments using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop GPUs demonstrate up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1-26.9% lower optimizer-step latency. The implementation also eliminates approximately 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per optimizer step. Numerical validation confirms consistency within the predefined FP32 tolerance, while convergence accuracy remains comparable across evaluated datasets and random seeds. These findings demonstrate that CUDA kernel fusion can substantially accelerate second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's underlying mathematical formulation and learning behavior.

title: Galop: Billion-Scale Genetic Programming on a Single GPU
abstract: Genetic programming (GP) evolves populations of heterogeneous programs, whereas GPUs achieve their highest throughput when groups of threads execute the same instructions. To better align GP evaluation with GPU execution, we present Galop, a hybrid CPU-GPU linear GP system that assigns one individual to each CUDA warp, a group of 32 threads that execute the same instructions across different fitness cases. We compare Galop against EvoGP, a recent high-performance GPU-based tree GP system, on data-rich symbolic regression across two unique GPUs, varying population size and fitness-case count. Galop completes evolutionary runs faster than EvoGP in 27 of the 28 main comparisons, with speedups of up to 13.6 times. Solution quality comparisons favour EvoGP overall, although Galop remains competitive on several problems. Galop also completes a full generation with 2.15 billion individuals on a single H100 GPU, approximately 4.0 times the largest population achieved by any other tested GP system. All five runs at this population complete 100 generations, with a median wall-clock time of 2.23 hours. These results make it practical to study GP populations in the billions on a single GPU. Galop's source code, experimental data, and reproducibility scripts are publicly available at this https URL.

title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

title: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance
abstract: We present a GPU-CPU hybrid framework for Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMAX-SAT) that complements state-of-the-art CPU solvers with differentiable GPU optimization. The GPU stage directly optimizes instance-specific categorical decision parameters without a training dataset or a pretrained predictive model. The central challenge in extending differentiable optimization to WPMAX-SAT is the hard/soft clause asymmetry: hard clauses represent inviolable feasibility constraints while soft clauses carry weights. We introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective, ensuring that GPU gradient descent leans towards the constraint structure of WPMAX-SAT.
